metadata.title: Measuring the civic duty to vote: A proposal

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses a cross-national internet survey administered immediately after the 2014 European Parliament election in seven countries (France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Austria, Greece, Portugal). The paper reports that samples were drawn from existing online panels with random selection of email addresses, stratified by region, and corrected using sex, age, and social-status quotas; however, it does not report the use of any explicit survey weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight scheme. Because the analysis is based on confirmatory factor analysis and related validity tests rather than ILSA achievement PV estimation, there is no PV-specific weighting requirement. Consequently, the manuscript provides quota-based balancing but does not document complex-survey weight application for estimation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the dependent constructs are attitudinal/psychometric measures of civic duty to vote (latent factor scores from CFA) and turnout (self-reported voting behavior), not cognitive achievement scores generated via PVs. The paper instead uses multiple Bayesian imputations to address missing questionnaire responses before estimating the CFA/SEM-style models. Therefore, PV handling is not part of the methodological pipeline for this study.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample for the full 13-indicator CFA is N=22,072 individuals across seven West European countries surveyed online immediately after the 2014 European Parliament election. The paper states that samples were drawn from existing online panels with random selection of email addresses, stratified by region, and quota-corrected on sex, age, and social status; it also reports dropout during the questionnaire of about 5% overall (higher in Austria and Greece). For the CFA estimation, the authors report applying multiple Bayesian imputation because missing data prevented computing modification indices and other estimation methods; they note missingness was not more than 5% of the total sample, and listwise deletion was justified but they still used Bayesian imputation. For the OLS concurrent validity tests, the paper explicitly reports listwise deletion of missing data.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 the study leveraged Political interest, Parents said voting duty, Age to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This paper proposes and validates a psychometric battery to measure civic duty to vote using a cross-national internet survey conducted immediately after the 2014 European Parliament election in seven countries (France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Austria, Greece, Portugal). The authors estimate an extended 13-indicator CFA model and then construct a reduced 4-indicator battery (CHOICE, GUILT, OPINION, COUNTRY), using multiple Bayesian imputations for missing responses. Model fit improves in the reduced model (RMSEA = .069; CFI = .98; df = 2; N = 22,072). For predictive validity, the duty latent construct is related to turnout (voted vs abstained) with standardized regression weights varying by country; the model shows good fit in each country (RMSEA never exceeding .08; CFI never below .94). Concurrent validity is tested via OLS regressions where political interest, parents’ socialization, and age explain between 15% and 26% of variation in the duty scale, with listwise deletion for missing data. Limitations include that the study is not an ML prediction paper and does not use survey-weight variables explicitly in the reported estimation pipeline. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This is not an empirical machine-learning prediction study using ILSA microdata; it is a construct validity and measurement-invariance study using CFA/SEM-style psychometric modeling on survey responses. As a result, there are no ML algorithms to extract (ml_techniques is empty) and there are no PV-based achievement outcomes to map to ILSA-style predictive targets. The paper’s main empirical outputs are CFA fit indices (RMSEA/CFI), factor loadings, and validity tests against turnout and related correlates.
